newsitem.title: USA: Storm leaves trail of destruction in New England.
newsitem.headline: Storm leaves trail of destruction in New England.

text.p: The storm that soaked parts of the New England with more than a foot-and-a-half (0.5 meter) of rain, caused damages estimated "in the tens of millions" of dollars, officials said on Tuesday.

The slow-moving coastal storm produced a 36-hour pounding torrent of water that damaged bridges, washed out highways, flooded homes, closed businesses and left more than 100,000 without drinking water.

Massachusetts officials said eastern communities including Boston suffered "tens of millions" in damages. New Hampshire suffered a "rough preliminary estimate of $5 million to $7 million in damages," according to the governor's office.

In Maine, which received some of the highest rainfall totals, the governor's office estimated damages of "at least $10 million," and said a request for federal emergency assistance was being prepared.

"I did see something in (the town of) Wells that I've never seen in my life, a snow plough clearing seaweed off the roads," Maine Gov. Angus King told reporters after touring the damage area by helicopter.

Flooding broke the primary supply pipe of the Portland Water District, leaving 140,000 residents of the state's largest city and surrounding communities without drinking water Tuesday. A boil-water order was expected to continue until Thursday.
Police in Saco, Maine, searched for a driver swept from his pickup truck. The storm was blamed for four deaths in the three days in battered the northeastern United States.

Authorities in New Hampshire kept a close eye on the Saco and Lamprey rivers that were above flood stage. The Concord, Nashua, Charles and Merrimack rivers seeped over their banks in Massachusetts flooding several communities north of Boston.
Dams also remained a concern in northern New England. Residents near Highland Lake in Westbrook, Maine, were urged to evacuate after water began flowing around the lake's dam.
Portland received 12.27 inches (29.7 cm) of rain from the storm that began late Sunday -- three times what it normally gets in the entire month of October.

Camp Ellis received 19.19 inches (48.7 cm) rain from the storm, which was "perhaps the greatest storm total since precipitation records have been established for Maine," the National Weather Service declared.
The old Yankee phrase "You can't get there from here" took on a new meaning in the storm's wake. Several washouts were reported on the Maine Turnpike - the state's primary north-south highway.
In Boston portions of the subway system remained closed because of flood damage to Kenmore Square, an important junction, which remained under water, a day after the storm left the city.

Emergency shelters remained open in several communities, but not everyone heeded evacuation calls. "I'd go with the house if it went," boasted Harry Ivers, who has lived along the Mill Brook in Westbrook, Maine, for 28 years.

The Portland-area's water system problems meant a busy day for the Poland Spring bottle water company. The Poland, Maine, firm delivered an extra 25,000 gallons to stores and donated 48,000 gallons to area hospitals that lacked drinking water.
